title: Bells
hookLine: church bells call to Mass, ring the Angelus and toll for the dead

lines: NOON. A BELL IN THE TOWER.
cards: Noon on a weekday. In a town square, a bell starts up in the church tower: a few strokes, a pause, a few more. A woman at a café table sets her cup down.
A man unloading a van stops, a box in his arms. Others keep walking. The bell rings either way.
The painter Jean-François Millet caught that moment in a field, in a canvas called The Angelus: two farm workers, a pitchfork and a basket at their feet, heads bowed while a far-off steeple rings.
A bell can't say a single word. It can only call.

teach.h: A BELL CALLS PEOPLE TO MASS.
teach.b: You met the Angelus prayer back on day one hundred three. In a Catholic parish, the bell has jobs. It calls people to Mass: when it rings before the liturgy, everyone in earshot knows the doors are open.
It rings the Angelus, named for the prayer's first Latin words, Angelus Domini, the angel of the Lord.
The prayer walks through the Annunciation, with Mary's words at its heart, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word."

teach.h: THE ANGELUS: THE WORD MADE FLESH.
teach.b: Then a line from John's Gospel: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Tradition rings it morning, noon and evening, so an ordinary day gets stitched, again and again, to the moment God came close.

teach.h: A SLOW TOLL FOR THE DEAD.
teach.b: And it tolls for the dead. Slow strokes, spaced far apart, tell the street that someone has died or is being buried. Nobody has to post a notice; the neighbors know to pray.

There's a smaller bell inside, too. The Church's instructions for Mass allow a server to ring it just before the consecration, and again as the priest lifts the host and then the chalice. Heads come up.
Then there's the week the bells go quiet.

teach.h: SILENT FROM HOLY THURSDAY TO EASTER.
teach.b: On Holy Thursday they ring out during the Gloria, and after that the Missal has them fall silent, all through Good Friday.

teach.h: BE IT DONE TO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.
teach.b: They come back at the Easter Vigil, when the Gloria is sung again. For a few days, the silence does the calling.

how: Catholic parishes may ring a bell before Mass, and some still ring the Angelus in the morning, at noon and in the evening, when people who hear it may stop to pray it. Bells are tolled for funerals, a small bell may be rung at the consecration, and the bells fall silent from the Gloria of Holy Thursday until the Gloria of the Easter Vigil.

o: a signal rung only once a Mass is over
a call to Mass, to the Angelus, to pray for the dead
a warning rung only for storms and for fires

games.q: what the bells say — tap the pairs.
p: the Annunciation, prayed through the day

s: church bells are only rung to call people to Mass
they also ring the Angelus and toll for the dead.
at Mass, a server may ring a small bell at the consecration
the Church's instructions for Mass allow it before the consecration and at each elevation.
church bells ring all through Holy Week, louder each day
after the Gloria on Holy Thursday they fall silent, and return at the Gloria of the Easter Vigil.

games.q: it's Holy Thursday evening. the Gloria begins and every bell in the church rings out. what happens to the bells next?
o: they ring every hour through the night.
they fall silent until the Gloria of the Easter Vigil.
they're rung only once more, for Good Friday's procession.
games.why: the Missal has them go quiet after the Gloria. they don't ring again until the Gloria is sung at the Easter Vigil, so for a few days, silence does the calling.

practice: Let the app's bell be your church bell: when it sounds, stop whatever your hands were about to do, and let your shoulders drop. If you pray, say the Angelus, or only Mary's line, be it done to me according to thy word.
If you don't, simply notice where you are, who is near, and what this hour is holding.

wordCard.voice: Bells. In a Catholic parish, the sound that calls people to Mass, rings the Angelus, and tolls for the dead, and that falls silent from Holy Thursday until Easter. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, "the angel of the Lord," the first words of the prayer the noon bell rings for.

carryVoice: Your line: the bell calls. It can't say a word, and still the whole street knows what it means. Until tomorrow.
